title: After the Sunset
full_review:
In director Brett Ratner's new caper comedy, "After the Sunset" (New Line), Woody Harrelson's beleaguered FBI agent divides the world's population into two distinct groups: "Those who like watching sunsets and those who don't."

Moviegoers may find themselves equally split between those who view films like this as diversionary popcorn fun and those who see them as derivative drivel, or worse, as glamorizing crime.

Sporting beach-bum scruff, Pierce Brosnan plays Max Burdett, a master thief with a sweet tooth for the Napoleon diamonds (three golf-ball-sized jewels which adorned the hilt of the legendary Corsican's sword). Having already pilfered two of the gaudy gems, Max and sexy accomplice Lola (Salma Hayek) call it quits and retire to a life of luxury on a tropical island where the only rock Lola wants to think about is the one that comes attached to an engagement ring.

But all play and no work makes Max a restless boy. Unable to kick the habit, he gets quick fixes by picking the pockets of unsuspecting couples over dinner at the beachfront resort.

Harrelson plays Stan, an inept G-man who's made a career out of trying to nab Max, with all the success of Wile E. Coyote trying to catch the Road Runner. Tracking Max down to his Bahamian hideaway, Stan drops the bait that one of the cruise ships in port is housing a rare jewel exhibit headlined by the third -- and sole remaining -- Napoleon diamond, betting the farm that Max will be unable to resist the itch of one last score. Helping Stan is Sophie (Naomie Harris), a beautiful local cop with whom he becomes romantically involved.

While the likable knave has long been a staple in the canon of caper cinema, it is understandable if some viewers find it difficult to root for a character who is, by all accounts, a common thief. And though some moral inroads are made late in the game, he remains, by and large, unreformed and unrepentant, taking particular glee in stealing and leaving the law holding the bag.
Whether or not Max will end up on the beach with Lola and an umbrella drink is never much in doubt; still, the film's ending seems to make light of the felonies committed and suggests that crime pays quite handsomely. As for the diamond, no spoilers here.

Even without his Aston Martin and 007 tux, Brosnan oozes roguish charm, an asset when trying to make a scoundrel like Max appealing. However, much of his performance seems retread from burglar roles in past movies such as 1999's remake of "The Thomas Crown Affair" and "The Tailor of Panama." Hayek has proved in films like "Frida" that she is more than just eye candy, but here she is reduced to curvy set-dressing, prancing around in increasingly revealing bikinis (pushing the envelope of the picture's PG-13 rating).

Unlike the purloined diamonds, the script is anything but flawless, detouring into subplots that go nowhere, including one involving an island kingpin (Don Cheadle). Also, the final jewel heist lacks any real tension. Still the film has its strengths, including good cat-and-mouse chemistry between Brosnan and Harrelson and some clever references to movies like "Jaws" and "Raiders of the Lost Ark."

In the final analysis, however, "After the Sunset" filches freely from past heist flicks (double-dealings, deftly choreographed capers, etc.) without ever really contributing anything new or innovative to the genre.

Due to a glamorized portrayal of larceny, crime without consequence, brief violence, several implied sexual encounters and some racy images, as well as an instance of rough language and intermittent crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
